title: load-profile-stability-experiments
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a set of experimental notes, load-profile definitions, and repeatability checks we ran to reduce variance in throughput measurements for the serving runtime. The focus is on: configuring load generators, choosing warmup policies that produce stable steady-state throughput, and capturing lightweight profiling signals to isolate bottlenecks.

Scope / Motivation:
- We observed 8-20% run-to-run throughput variance across nominally identical runs.
- Need a repeatable procedure that productizes into CI-level smoke tests and longer nightly sweeps.
- Want to separate hardware-induced variance (PCIe, NUMA) from runtime-level effects (batching, KV cache priming, kernel stalls).

High-level recommendations (summary):
- Use a two-phase measurement: warmup until 95% throughput plateau, then steady-state window of 3–5 minutes.
- Record system-level counters continuously (GPU util, SM efficiency, memory bw, CPU p95, interrupts) and attach to each run.
- Use deterministic core pinning and disable frequency scaling on measurement hosts to reduce jitter.
- For small models / short sequences, explicitly prefill KV-cache or run a short token-prefill phase to avoid first-request penalties.

Load profiles used in experiments (kept small & representative):
- profile-short: seq_len=64 (mean), tokens_per_request=64, request_rate sweep {50,100,200,400} req/s, target_concurrency sweep {1..16}
- profile-mid: seq_len=256 (mean), tokens_per_request=256, request_rate sweep {10,20,40,80} req/s, concurrency {1..8}
- profile-long: seq_len=1024 (mean), tokens_per_request=1024, request_rate sweep {1,2,4,8} req/s, concurrency {1..4}
- mixed: 60% short / 30% mid / 10% long, Poisson arrival with per-request token variance ±25%

Warmup methodology (detailed):
1) Phase 0 - cold check (optional): single synthetic request, measure cold latency, and note kernel load times.
2) Phase 1 - linear ramp: start at 5% of target rate and ramp linearly to target over 30s. Purpose: avoid immediate overload and observe ramp behaviour.
3) Phase 2 - steady fill: hold target rate for a minimum 120s. Monitor instantaneous throughput every 5s.
4) Plateau detection: compute rolling 30s mean throughput; consider plateau reached when the last three rolling means differ by <2%.
5) Steady-state measurement: once plateau reached, record a 180s window for final metrics. If plateau not reached after 6 minutes, fail the run and capture diagnostics.

Why plateau detection?
- Some kernels (KV cache priming, JIT-like kernels, lazy allocator paths) take tens of seconds to converge. Simple fixed warmup durations exhibit under- or over-warmup for different models and hardware.

Repeatability controls (host & runtime):
- CPU: isolate 2 logical cores per GPU for runtime housekeeping, pin loadgen worker threads to other isolated cores. Use nohz_full and isolcpus on Linux where possible.
- Governor: set CPU governor to performance and fix GPU persistence_mode=1 for NVIDIA.
- NUMA: pin model-serving process memory to the GPU-attached NUMA node. Export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES explicitly.
- Containers: run with --privileged=false but with CAP_SYS_NICE where necessary; avoid noisy co-tenants on test hosts.
- Kernel tuning: set swappiness low, reduce ASLR where necessary for exact-matching tests, but avoid making this the default for CI (documented as optional).

Loadgen configuration examples (internal test harness):
- baseline command (pseudo): rwl-run --profile profile-mid --target-rate 40 --max-concurrency 8 --ramp 30 --prefill-kv true --metrics-interval 5 --plateau-threshold 0.02 --plateau-window 30 --steady-window 180 --output-json out.json
- Dockerized execution: docker run --rm --cpuset-cpus=\"4-11\" --env CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 redwood/loadgen:ci rwl-run ...

Essential metrics to capture per run (capture every 1s or 5s):
- app: requests/s, tokens/s, mean latency, p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, error-rate
- gpu: utilization %, SM efficiency, memory bandwidth (GB/s), L2 hit rate (if available), GPU temperature, power
- kernel: % time waiting on cudaEvent vs compute, kernel occupancy, average grid size
- system: CPU steal, irq rate, context-switch rate, major page faults, network RX/TX throughput, disk IO
- runtime: queue lengths (pre-kernel and post-kernel), batching distribution (batch size histogram), KV cache hit ratio, average cache fill time

Profiling hooks (lightweight):
- Periodic cudaProfiler sampling (not full nvprof) for 10s during steady window.
- Insert sparse tracing boundaries to mark request lifecycle (recv -> tokenize -> preproc -> enqueue -> kernel -> postproc -> send).
- Capture a single in-depth run with nsight systems for 60s for any failing or high-variance cases.

Observed failure modes and troubleshooting notes (empirical):
- High variance late in run: often correlated with CPU frequency scaling or background cron jobs. Check dmesg and /proc/interrupts.
- Throughput dip after large-request: KV cache invalidation on eviction thresholds; fix by increasing cache size or using controlled eviction policy for tests.
- Spiky latency with high concurrency: queueing in loadgen or on the host IO subsystem; observe sockfd queue lengths and netstat output.
- First 20s lower throughput: allocator warmup in the runtime; prefill helps.
- GPU underutilized despite high request rate: small batches (batch size 1) cause kernel launch overheads. Use fused kernels or increase batching window.

Example experimental sweep (what we ran):
- For each model variant (fp16, int8-quant): for each profile in {short, mid, long, mixed}: run rate sweep to find knee point (where latency rises >2x p95). For each knee point setting run 5 repeated runs with full capture. Compute mean and coefficient of variation for tokens/s across repeats.
- Result snapshot: int8 variants had 12% higher nominal throughput but 2x higher variance on short sequences due to different kernel selection paths.

Artifacts & outputs we store per run (mandatory):
- out.json (summary metrics), timeline.systrace (if taken), nvml.csv (1s samples), loadgen.log (full stdout/stderr), host_dmesg.txt, /proc/interrupts snapshot, nsight-report (if executed).

Actionable mitigations for the most common problems:
- If variance caused by CPU hustle: pin threads + set performance governor + run on isolated nodes.
- If warmup plateau not reached: enable KV prefill or extend plateau window; add a prewarm phase that sends N silence requests to populate caches.
- If kernel selection oscillates: pin a kernel profile via config (force path) for benchmarking; follow up with kernel selection fixes in runtime.

Next steps / experiments to try:
- Nightly deterministic benchmark that runs the mixed profile with pinned cores and collects 50 repeats for statistical monitoring.
- Microbenchmark for kernel launch overhead vs batch size on each supported GPU family.
- Injected-noise experiments: schedule a synthetic CPU stressor to quantify sensitivity to co-located noisy neighbors.

Appendix: Quick reproducible checklist for an engineer
- Step 1: Reserve an isolated test host with no other workloads.
- Step 2: Set CPU governor and GPU persistence.
- Step 3: Checkout branch redwood/serving-runtime@benchmarks/load-stability.
- Step 4: Run prefill: rwl-run --profile profile-mid --prefill-kv true --target-rate 20 --ramp 10 --steady-window 60
- Step 5: Run full-sweep: rwl-run --profile mixed --sweep-kv --repeat 5 --output outdir/$(date +%F)/
- Step 6: Upload artifacts to the benchmark bucket and attach JIRA INF-7421.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic and mixes heuristics with measured practices. The plateau detector is conservative; we prefer slightly longer windows over optimistic short warmups.
- For CI use, shorten windows but mark as smoke tests only; nightly runs must keep current windows.

End of doc.
